text: - That the Bail Act 1985 be amended to preclude the granting of bail in cases of alleged domestic violence, such as assault on a family member, by any bail authority other than a Court;
- That all cases of alleged domestic violence, such as an assault on a family member, be in any event brought before a Magistrates Court within 48 hours of the arrest of the alleged perpetrator;

- That the Bail Act 1985 be amended so as to require in any bail agreement in cases of alleged domestic violence, such as assault on a family member, a condition in the same terms as the ‘firearms term’ as set out in the Intervention Orders (Prevention of Abuse) Act 2009; Response from the Attorney-General      The Government is currently reviewing aspects of the Bail Act and has taken the Coroner’s recommendations into account. Further, I note that the final recommendation accords with the intent of other legislation implemented by the Government regarding the use of weapons and firearms. The Intervention Orders (Prevention of Abuse) Act 2009 came into effect on 9 December 2011 and the Statutes Amendment (Serious Firearm Offences) Act 2012 came into effect on 4 March 2013 creating a separate category of offenders called “serious firearms offenders”. This established a presumption against bail for serious firearm offenders. In addition, any offender who is granted bail is now subject to a condition prohibiting the person from possessing any firearm, part of a firearm or any ammunition will form part of the bail agreement. - That the Medical Director of the South Australian Prison Health Service assign to a senior medical officer or officers within the Service the responsibility of maintaining oversight of the medical treatment and investigation of those prisoners within institutions operated by the Department for Correctional Services who are suspected of suffering from a serious or life threatening illness, especially in circumstances where the medical treatment and investigation of such prisoners is being conducted by medical practitioners who are not employees of the Service.      A memo has been distributed to all senior medical practitioners within the South Australian Prison Health Service (SAPHS) to ensure that they are reminded of their responsibility for the oversight of the medical treatment and investigation of those prisoners within their care.      In addition, to improve the clinical care of those prisoners within institutions operated by the Department for Correctional Services (DCS), SAPHS is working with the Central Adelaide Local Health Network (CALHN) to implement a number of strategies intended to redesign the current model of care provided. This is being progressed in association with DCS. The following two initiatives have been identified as major reforms for implementation in 2013/2014:    The Two Stage Admission Process initiative promotes a more structured approach to the assessment of patients health needs by ensuring that a more comprehensive risk assessment is undertaken. Patients are triaged, resulting in appropriate referral and a more cohesive approach to health care management.    The Medications in Possession initiative allows prisoners to access their medications and have responsibility for their administration, the same way they would manage their health care if living in the community (with some exclusions, e.g. drugs of dependence). The implementation of this initiative will significantly reduce the time spent on administering medications, allowing for a shift in focus to chronic disease care planning and improved discharge planning.

- That the Medical Director of the South Australian Prison Health Service remind medical practitioners, both employed within the Service or otherwise, who treat prisoners within institutions operated by the Department for Correctional Services of the need to carefully explain to prisoners who are for whatever reason reluctant to undergo important medical treatment or investigation of the possible consequences of the failure of the prisoner to undergo such treatment or investigation and in particular to identify to the particular prisoner the worst case scenario that such an investigation might identify.      The SAPHS Clinical Director distributed a memo on 27 March, 2013, to all SAPHS employed Medical Officers and Clinical Service Coordinators (to distribute to Medical Officers not employed with SAPHS) which stated: “In line with coronial recommendations all medical practitioners are reminded that:    Imprisonment does not negate a patient’s right to refuse treatment or to refuse to accept medical recommendations.    Whenever a patient refuses: Annual Report of the State Coroner 2013-2014                                                                 Page 35    Assess his/her mental state to determine if he/she is capable of making an informed decision.    Counsel the patient on the potential benefits and risks of either accepting or declining to accept your recommendation.    The Department for Health and Ageing requires you to ask the patient to sign an Acknowledgement of Medical Advice form when you are of the opinion that refusal is likely to adversely affect him/her.    Document the conversation and the patient’s reasons for refusal in his/her medical file.    Inform nursing staff during your hand over at the end of clinic.    DCS should be informed if refusal is likely to affect their management of the patient.”

- That the Medical Director of the South Australian Prison Health Service remind medical practitioners, both employed within the Service or otherwise, of the need to make detailed notations in a prisoner patient’s clinical record of the decision made by the prisoner not to undergo recommended medical treatment or investigation and of the stated reason for the prisoner refusing to undergo such medical treatment or investigation.      Refer to recommendations 2 and 4.

- That the Medical Director of the South Australian Prison Health Service and the Chief Executive Officer of the Department for Correctional Services be mindful of the fact that a refusal by a prisoner situated in a country correctional facility to undergo medical treatment or investigation that requires the prisoner to travel to Adelaide does not of itself mean that the prisoner cannot at least be compelled to travel to Adelaide and be accommodated in a correctional facility in Adelaide. Subsequent action by SA Health      SAPHS have implemented a written “advice of medical appointment” system at the Port Augusta Prison which will roll out to all sites. This will give the patient the opportunity to advise SAPHS directly of their intent to attend or not attend their health appointments. Subsequently, SAPHS can document this appropriately and provide the patient with advice on the consequences of non- attendance. Irrespective of whether or not the patient intends to keep their appointment, SAPHS will maintain the appointment and request the transfer of the prisoner to attend the appointment.      SAPHS is also implementing strategies for improved patient access and investigating improved processes for:    how prisoners should request an appointment with health    how prisoners are advised of their scheduled appointment    how prisoners can cancel a health appointment  prisoner responsibility to confirm intent to attend a health appointment. Subsequent action by the Department for Correctional Services      I am advised that SAPHS have now implemented an ‘Advice of Medical Appointment’ form at Port Augusta Prison. This new form will give a prisoner the opportunity to advise SAPHS directly on their intent to attend, or not attend, a health appointment.      Irrespective of the wishes of the prisoner, SAPHS have undertaken to keep the medical appointment booked (as arranged) and will still request the transfer of the prisoner to attend the appointment. This will allow for a final discussion to take place with the prisoner who will be requested to confirm if he/she wishes to attend the appointment or not.

- That the Medical Director of the South Australian Prison Health Service and the Chief Executive Officer of the Department for Correctional Services make every effort to ensure that the conditions enjoyed by a prisoner in a country correctional facility are not in any way jeopardised by the need for the prisoner to travel to Adelaide and be accommodated in an Adelaide correctional facility for the purpose of attending medical treatment or investigation in Adelaide.      Whilst prisoner placement is at the discretion of DCS, SAPHS offers advice to DCS on the placement of prisoners with special health needs and those transferring through the prison system for health appointments. Furthermore, SAPHS advises DCS regarding those prisoners who are likely to be adversely affected by refusing treatment. SAPHS also advises DCS if refusal is based on the perception of a potential loss of privileges. This process is documented in accordance with the SA Health Providing Medical Assessment and/or Treatment where Consent cannot be obtained policy directive and associated guidelines.      Advice received from DCS is that “It is recommended that a Statewide Operations Deputy Chief Executive Notification is created and issued stipulating the following: 1. Where possible, the Department for Correctional Services will facilitate requests from South Australian Prison Health Service for a prisoner to travel from a regional correctional facility to Adelaide for the purpose of attending medical treatment or a medical appointment. 2. Consideration is given for the prisoner to return to the same regional correctional facility where possible. 3. Demonstrate that DCS has given consideration to the placement of a prisoner for a medical appointment or medical treatment in Adelaide making every effort to ensure conditions enjoyed by a prisoner in a country correctional facility are not in any way jeopardised. 4. All factors have been taken into consideration for the transfer of the prisoner from a regional correctional facility to Adelaide.” Subsequent action by the Department for Correctional Services      SAPHS provides advice to the Department with regard to the placement of prisoners with special

- That the Commissioner of Police allocate proper resources to ensure that high risk offenders have dedicated case managers and, as far as is practicable, that the same case manager monitor high risk offenders throughout their time under ANCOR.      The Sexual Crime Investigation Branch (SCIB) monitors compliance with the obligations imposed on such offenders by the Child Sex Offender Registration Act 2006 with individual investigators monitoring an average 10 to 12 people. Medium and low risk offenders are monitored by Local Service Areas. Country Local Service Areas assist with the day to day management of people residing in country, regional and remote locations. As far as practicable, offenders are monitored by the same investigator but changes do occur due to circumstances such as staff transfers. The 2013/14 State Budget provisions for recruitment of 50 additional police will allow five new positions to be allocated to the ANCOR Unit within SCIB which will, amongst other outcomes, support monitoring capacity.

- That the Commissioner of Police formally advises ANCOR staff and Officers of their obligations to the protection of children.     In particular the requirement to make mandatory notifications of suspected risk, to share information and negotiate with other agencies to effect the safe investigation of those concerns.      SAPOL uses General Orders as the formal framework for providing formal advice and direction to members. - That the Commissioner of Police ensure that all SAPOL call centre staff and officers should have specific and regular skills training and procedural updates to ensure they have a working knowledge of appropriate responses and their obligations relating to disclosures of domestic violence.      A substantially upgraded training programme for domestic violence and intervention orders has been developed and delivered to both sworn and unsworn Call Centre staff. The initial course comprises three 45 minute sessions, with annual 30 minute refresher sessions to be conducted thereafter. It highlights the need for positive action to be taken on all reports of domestic abuse, reinforcing instructions contained in SAPOL's Domestic Violence Policing Model and General Order, Domestic Abuse. The training emphasises that in all instances when a report of domestic violence is received by telephone, a patrol should be dispatched unless:      it can be clearly established that the reported offence/incident is historical; and      the victim is in no immediate or foreseeable danger; and      the matter can reasonably be reported by the victim in person to a police station.      The concern expressed by the Coroner over the manner in which the Call Centre carried out its duties at that time is acknowledged by SAPOL. The resultant remedial training programme as discussed above was developed and implemented prior to the Inquest. Advice of those actions was provided to the Inquest by both affidavit and oral testimony.      Recommendation 3 had already been essentially addressed prior to the Inquest.      A policy Domestic Abuse has been developed for SAPOL's Communications Group (which includes the Call Centre) and came into operation on 22 April 2013. This specifically deals with the handling of telephone reports of domestic abuse and is supplementary to the above mentioned Domestic Violence Policing Model and General Order, Domestic abuse. Since May 2013, domestic violence training has also included input from SAPOL's Victim Policy State Coordinator. - Call centre staff who are administrative officers (not members of the police force) should not be allowed to make “cold calls” to victims of domestic violence. Such contacts should only be made by phone by appropriately trained police officers.      The intent of this recommendation is understood. However, if SAPOL were to apply the recommendation in all circumstances, it would prevent non-sworn Call Centre operators from contacting victims under any circumstances. This recommendation has been applied consistently with SAPOL's Communications Group Local Policy "Domestic Abuse" which came into effect in April 2013. This provides that the Call Centre supervisors, who are all sworn police officers, are in the best position to make appropriate decisions on the methodology for contacting victims in each particular instance. To that end, Call Centre operators are required to seek the advice from their supervisor whenever possible prior to making any contact with the victim. Subsequent action by the Department for Correctional Services Mr Robinson’s death was a catalyst for a number of improvements in the way that the Department manages offenders in the community. Soon after the incident, the Department initiated a Parole Improvement Project and engaged internal auditors from the Attorney-General’s Department to conduct a comprehensive review of controls over Parole supervision, and to also review Parole practices. The Department subsequently introduced the Enhanced Community Corrections model - a tiered supervision service standard that categorises offenders according to risk. The initiative is focused on targeting resources towards those offenders who present the highest risk of re-offending, and who pose the greatest threat to public safety. Within Enhanced Community Corrections there is a particular focus on:      Evidence based, effective supervision of offenders;      Strengthened compliance management and enforcement;      Improving links between Community Corrections and the Courts and the Parole Board; and      The effective use of electronic monitoring.

- That the Minister for Correctional Services implements a random saliva testing system based on the system employed by SAPOL for roadside testing of motorists as a supplement to the urinalysis testing presently used in the supervision of high risk parolees.      The Department has not implemented this recommendation.      Departmental investigations of the saliva based testing currently on the market (including the methods currently being utilised by SAPOL) determined that those devices were expensive and limited in use with regard to the number of drugs which were able to be detected. For example, the SAPOL devices can detect Cannabis and Amphetamines only. Urine testing can detect up to nine different drug types.      Urinalysis is able to detect a broader history of drug use compared to saliva based tests. A urinalysis can show an offender’s drug use days, even up to a month, prior to testing. In comparison, saliva-based testing has a narrower window of detection and can only show use of a drug within the preceding hours of the test.      Saliva based testing does not meet Departmental service delivery requirements. As part of the case management process, offenders are tested in line with their community based order conditions as well as the Operational Compliance Framework (created as part of Enhanced Community Corrections). The Framework ensures that positive urine results and other breaches are communicated within the specified time frames (for each tier).      It is noted that the Department is now utilising new ‘screening cups’ for the drug testing of offenders. The cups are easy to use and give accurate results within 5-10 minutes - achieving an efficient service with a reduction in laboratory costs. If the result shows a presumptive positive, a full confirmation is then arranged.

- That the Minister for Correctional Services ensures Community Corrections Staff are specifically trained in and cognisant of procedures relating to the disclosure of domestic violence offending by victims. This should include the ability to conduct standard risk assessment and effect relevant referrals including to a Family Safety Framework meeting where high risk is indentified. Annual Report of the State Coroner 2013-2014                                                                Page 41      DCS has acted in support of this recommendation.      The Department is currently reviewing how domestic violence training is delivered to staff across Community Corrections.      DCS has identified that it is critically important for staff to have access to quality training given the complex nature of domestic violence offending. This includes acknowledgment of the unique profile of domestic violence offenders as well as the specialist skills required to manage those offenders.      On 22 May 2013 a new chapter (‘Chapter 21’) was inserted into the Department’s Probation and Parole Guidelines which specifically outlines principles for supervision and intervention in relation to domestic Violence. Included within the new chapter is:    Detail with regard to identifying instances of domestic violence;    Outline of risk and safety (including additional assessment for risk of Domestic Violence);    Detail regarding limits of confidentiality;    Information on relevant intervention and support programs,    Outline of specific case management requirements for Domestic Violence offenders; and    Detail with regard to risk assessment and the Family Safety Framework.      To this end, Chapter 21 also states that Community Corrections Officers who work with domestic violence offenders should undertake training with regard to responding to domestic violence, intervention with men who are abusive and violent toward female partners and responding to women subjected to domestic abuse and violence. Community Correctional Officers should also seek advice/supervision from an experienced colleague. This is particularly important for Officers

- That the Department for Correctional Services continue to identify and eliminate hanging points from cells in all South Australian correctional institutions and, in particular, to replace all ventilation grilles, air-conditioning vents and similar with anti-ligature vents.      The Department has previously accepted Coroner’s recommendations in relation to potential ligature (hanging) points and continues (within existing resources) to modify infrastructure to remove or modify potential points based on an assessment of risk.      Over a number of years, the Department for Correctional Services (DCS) has been installing furniture and cell fixtures, which comply with safe cell design guidelines. This is in order to reduce the potential for prisoner self-harm.      The main focus is replacing existing cell bunks, shelving units and desks, with anti-ligature design equivalents.      These works have been funded on an annual basis from the Department’s capital budget. The cost to remove ligature points from prison cells varies from prison to prison and cell to cell. This depends on a number of variables, such as the existing style of showers and toilet facilities, beds, storage facilities and hand basins. As cells have different infrastructure, it is not possible to indicate a generic cost for a full ‘safe cell’ conversion.      In relation to the specific points identified as a result of this Inquiry, I can advise that approximately 50 per cent of the metal ventilation grilles above the cell doors in B Division of Yatala Labour Prison have been replaced as a priority, and this work is ongoing.      During 2013, works were also undertaken in all cells in Yatala Labour Prison’s G Division and I am pleased to confirm that all are now classified as meeting ‘safe cell’ standards.      All new secure custody cells constructed also meet “safe cell” specifications and ongoing works will be funded through future annual capital works programs to continue to reduce the ability for self- harm within the State’s prisons.

- That the Department for Correctional Services take the necessary steps to ensure that prisoners do not have an ability to hoard or stockpile excessive quantities of prescribed or illicitly obtained medication in their cells.       In this regard consideration should be given to the implementation of random cell searches in order to deter such hoarding or stockpiling.      The Department for Correctional Services is committed to keeping prisoners, staff and the community safe. As part of this commitment, the Department is dedicated in its efforts to stop the supply and trafficking of drugs in prison. The Department deploys a range of measures to reduce trafficking through targeting and minimising supply and demand, and undertakes a number of targeted and random, whole of institution searches.          Searches of this nature are generally a collaborative effort and can involve members of the Department’s Emergency Response Group, Operations Security Unit, Ethics, Intelligence and Investigations Unit, officers at each site, South Australian Police and the Australian Customs Service. Regular local search programs are also undertaken parallel to such whole of institution searches.      Pursuant to Section 37 of the Correctional Services Act 1982, the Manager of a correctional institution may cause a prisoner’s belongings to be searched for the purpose of detecting prohibited items. Further, subsequent to changes to the Correctional Services Act 1982 being enacted in August 2012, higher penalties exist in relation to the introduction of illicit drugs, and other prescribed prohibited items (including mobile telephones and weapons).              In the three financial years following Mr Smith’s death (2012-13; 2011-12; and 2010-11) over 185,000 searches were conducted on prisoner areas and their cells and property throughout the State’s prison Annual Report of the State Coroner 2013-2014                                                                 Page 43 system, resulting in excess of 1,100 drug and paraphernalia items being located and confiscated. In essence, the Department continues to strive to ensure that no prisoner has access to prohibited items, including prescription or illicitly obtained drugs whilst in the custody environment.      The South Australian Prison Health Service (SAPHS) (part of the Department of Health and Ageing) is responsible for the provision of health care services to all prisoners in State managed

- That the Department for Correctional Services continue to develop operating procedures that will ensure that evidence of a prisoner who is suspected of having attempted self harm is properly evaluated by the appropriate person or entity so as to eliminate the possibility that the attempt at self harm will not be properly identified or acted upon. In particular it should be regarded as inappropriate for agency nursing staff to make any such assessment without other professional assistance.      The Deputy Coroner’s recommendation referred to the need for other professionals to be involved in self-harm assessments – and that the Deputy Coroner considered it inappropriate for agency nursing staff to make such assessments without other professional assistance.      Advice obtained from SAPHS is that health assessments are undertaken by suitably qualified health staff. The skill level and knowledge base of agency nursing staff determines if they have the ability to undertake an assessment within the prison environment. When requesting agency nursing staff, priority is given to those staff who have prior experience in the corrections environment or who have a background in mental health, drug and alcohol or emergency nursing. All nursing staff are provided with an orientation package detailing processes related to providing safe care within the corrections environment, including location and how to access SAPHS procedures and protocols. Orientation manuals are also available.      The Department for Correctional Services (DCS) acknowledges that the assessment and management of a prisoner’s risk of suicide or self-harm is a shared multi-disciplinary responsibility from the prisoner’s admission until discharge.      The DCS System Operating Procedure 90 (SOP 90) describes DCS responsibilities and resulting actions, to minimise the risk of prisoners attempting suicide or self-harm whilst in custody. An attachment to this SOP (Appendix 1) entitled Information and Characteristics of Self-Harm and Suicide provides further guidance to staff in making such a determination.      The SOP was developed in 2011, and makes specific reference to departmental staff responsibilities including Correctional Officers and other employees and their responsibility in raising a formal

- That the Department for Correctional Services implement procedures whereby prisoners on remand are regularly formally screened for risk of self harm. Such screening procedures could occur at times when a remand prisoner is returned from Court or where some other identifiable adverse change of circumstance has occurred in respect of that prisoner. I repeat the recommendation made in the Inquest into the death of Damian John Cook, namely that the Department for Correctional Services establish a panel to examine the feasibility of introducing a regime whereby inmates at South Australian correctional institutions are formally screened for risk of self harm on a more regular basis than at the time of their entry into an institution.      The comments in relation to recommendation three are also relevant to this recommendation. SOP 90 describes how at-risk prisoners returning from court, police escorts, medical appointments, compassionate leave, or upon transfer in from other prison locations must be observed to ensure the wellbeing of the prisoner and if there are any signs of distress. If a staff member has reported any concerns regarding the prisoner, their risk status is to be formally assessed by SAPHS staff or the Responsible Officer and follow up care provided through the prison’s HRAT as appropriate.      This SOP previously included the requirement that all HRAT prisoners be formally screened upon their return from Court. However, following consultation with the Public Service Association (PSA) this requirement was reduced to only being HRAT prisoners who showed signs of distress. In this regard, PSA had indicated that it would have industrial related concerns if all prisoners returning from court required formal screening.      G4S (escorting officers) staff are required however, to note any concerns noted during an escort. This in turn would result in a Notice of Concern being raised and formal risk assessment undertaken in accordance with the SOP.

- That in respect of a prisoner incarcerated in South Australia, the Department for Correctional Services routinely make enquires of the equivalent Departments in other States and Territories as to the history of risk of self-harm in respect of that prisoner during any period of incarceration in those other States and Territories.      In an effort to give the appropriate level of consideration to this recommendation, the Department for Correctional Services raised it through the Corrective Services Administrators’ Council (CSAC) for exploration and discussion.      Advice from interstate jurisdictions is that there are already mechanisms in place through existing legislative provisions to share information of this nature between States and Territories. However, various barriers have been noted with regards to the suggestion of establishing a national approach ultimately aimed at addressing the concerns raised by the South Australian Deputy Coroner.      The first challenge remains that the State or Territory receiving the prisoner of concern needs to know that the prisoner has been incarcerated in another jurisdiction and therefore which State/s or Territory/ies to make enquiries with. Annual Report of the State Coroner 2013-2014                                                               Page 45      Current processes, as is the case in most jurisdictions such as South Australia, rely on the self-disclosure of information relating to a prisoner having any prior criminal history or episode of suicide attempts and/or self-harming behaviour in the first instance.      Impediments also include likely significant resource impacts for Departments, in obtaining such information for every prisoner entering the prison system and in responding to other jurisdictions in a timely fashion. In this regard, it is considered that the staff resources required to seek and obtain such information from a particular jurisdiction, and alternatively, to retrieve and provide to a requesting jurisdiction for all prisoners entering the prison system on a national basis would be both overly resource intensive and largely unnecessary.      Furthermore, if jurisdictions were to progress the Deputy Coroner’s recommendation for only prisoners identified as being a risk of self-harm, this still would not have benefited Mr Smith in his

- That the Department for Correctional Services educate the prison population in this State to the effect that genuine expressions of concern in respect of their fellow prisoners, as imparted to persons in authority, will not involve adverse consequences either to the prisoner who is the subject of the report or to the reporting prisoner.      Suicide Awareness is an ongoing awareness program offered by the Department to staff. It also has a Peer Support Program in place at a number of prison sites, whereby identified prisoners are trained to support other prisoners with various issues associated with being incarcerated. The intent of the program is to keep at-risk prisoners, who may be reluctant to seek the assistance of professional care givers, safe and well during incarceration.       Empowering carefully selected, responsible prisoners with a peer supporting role employs a valuable, under-utilised resource. Case Managers work closely with these supporters to ensure positive outcomes. Annual Report of the State Coroner 2013-2014                                                                 Page 46      Notwithstanding the Peer Support Program already in place, investigations are being undertaken to identify further opportunities for information videos relating to peer support training to be shown to prisoners on the prisoner television channels.

- That the Department for Correctional Services give consideration to routinely accommodating remand prisoners at correctional institutions in close proximity to their families, taking into account the current stage which their matters have reached within the criminal justice system, the duration of the period on which they have been or are expected to be on remand, the availability of video conferencing as a means of securing their participation in court proceedings in which they are required to participate and the convenience of their legal advisers.      The Department does make every effort to accommodate prisoners in accordance with this recommendation. Other factors are also taken into consideration, including but not limited to matters such as future court appearances; the need for rehabilitation services; the security rating of the prisoner concerned; personal health needs; general safety concerns for the prisoner in terms of the existence of known prisoner enemies and/or any other special needs or considerations that may be relevant to that prisoner. Given the Department is experiencing unprecedented levels of prisoner numbers at this time this can further impact on prisoner placements.

- That the Minister for Correctional Services give consideration to revising the South Australian response to recommendation 168 of the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody to include remand prisoners within the recommendation’s field of operation, such that Correctional Services affect the placement and transfer of Aboriginal prisoners, both those on remand and those serving a sentence of imprisonment, according to the principle that, where possible, an Aboriginal prisoner should be placed in an institution as close as possible to the place of residence of his or her family.      With regard to prisoners being accommodated near their families, and as previously stated above, the location of family is already considered as part of placement deliberations. In particular, Aboriginal prisoners are kept close to family whenever the Department is able to facilitate such a placement. As noted however, placements may also be impacted by other factors that are equally as critical in ensuring their safe and secure management. In such cases, special care is taken to ensure regular contact with other incarcerated family members if relevant, or have regular, ongoing contact with the prison’s Aboriginal Liaison Officer.      The Department has also during 2012-13 established a pilot Elders Visitation Program at the Adelaide Women’s Prison, Mobilong Prison and Port Augusta Prison. This program aims at improving the reintegration prospects of Aboriginal offenders by maintaining links to community and culture while in prison. These goals directly respond to recommendations 168 and 169, which address the need for Aboriginal detainees to be accommodated in close proximity to their families. Further, recommendation 170, which recognises the family and kinship obligations of Aboriginal detainees which extend beyond immediate family and recommendation 183, which recognises the need for Aboriginal detainees to establish and maintain support groups within institutions and for community groups to provide educational and cultural services to Aboriginal detainees all relate to this recommendation and the goals associated with this program. It is envisaged at this time that given the successes of the pilot to date, the program will gradually be expanded to include other prison sites.
